analysis.investment_thesis: Aegis Logistics is a well-run terminal infrastructure play riding India's LPG penetration and chemical logistics growth, with net profit compounding at 22.6% CAGR over 9 years and a promoter firmly in control at 58.1%. The 32x P/E is not cheap, but the fee-based terminal model with high barriers to entry makes this a reasonable hold at current levels.
key_strengths: Promoter holding 58.1% — founder-led, aligned management with consistent capital allocation into terminal infrastructure
Operating income CAGR of 21.9% over 9 years despite revenue volatility (oil-price driven) — proves the fee-based terminal model's stability

India's LPG penetration and chemical logistics volume growth provides a decade-long structural demand tailwind; total assets nearly doubled in 2 years (FY23: 7,069 Cr → FY25: 12,050 Cr), reflecting aggressive terminal expansion
key_risks: Finance costs nearly doubled in 2 years (FY23: INR 88 Cr → FY25: INR 165 Cr) as debt expanded; total debt jumped to INR 4,606 Cr in FY25 — rising interest burden could pressure ROE below 15%
ROCE of 13.2% is modest for an infrastructure business requiring heavy ongoing capex (INR 945 Cr in FY25 alone)
Revenue is volatile (peaked at INR 8,627 Cr in FY23, fell to INR 6,764 Cr by FY25) as commodity throughput volumes fluctuate with oil prices — misleads on business quality
red_flags: Debt trajectory concerning: borrowings grew from INR 835 Cr (FY22) to INR 2,439 Cr (FY25) while total debt reported at INR 4,606 Cr — reconciliation gap needs scrutiny
FCF has been mostly negative (-386 Cr in FY25) due to massive capex spend; dividend sustainability depends on debt markets staying benign
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Aegis Logistics is a classic India infrastructure compounder — it doesn't look exciting on revenue (lumpy, oil-price sensitive) but the terminal throughput fees generate a resilient and growing operating income stream. The 22.6% net profit CAGR over 9 years is impressive, and the asset base expansion (terminals in Mumbai, Pipavav, Kochi) positions it well for the decade ahead as India's LPG and petrochemical logistics needs grow with urbanization and industrialization. The promoter's 58% stake gives me comfort on long-term alignment.

My hesitation is the rapidly expanding debt footprint — finance costs of INR 165 Cr in FY25 are growing at 27.9% CAGR, faster than profits, compressing returns. The massive capex cycle (INR 945 Cr in FY25) is necessary but is generating negative FCF and requires external financing. At 32x P/E and with rising leverage, this is not a screaming buy, but the terminal moat and India's energy logistics story keep it in the portfolio at current levels.
